abstract: Structural variants are a common cause of human diseases, but their detection from short-read sequencing remains challenging, despite being the technology underlying most clinical workflows. We present dicast, a machine-learning method that scores SV calls from short-read data using alignment and genomic-context features. dicast is trained on a new multi-technology ground truth built from nine samples, with extensive manual curation. It outperforms existing short-read callers and consensus approaches, recovering substantially more true positives at high precision. We also demonstrate dicast's applicability for diagnostics, identifying all pathogenic variants in multiple disease cohorts, and 20% more candidate pathogenic deletions than consensus approaches.

Ethics approval and consent to participate: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Samples first analyzed in Schöpflin et al. [32] were collected under the approvals stated therein. The study of the neuromuscular disease cohort was approved by the Ethics Review Board of the Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District, Helsinki University Hospital (HUS/16896/2022). The atrial fibrillation cohort was collected in a previously published study [71] under the ethical approvals reported there. Referring clinicians obtained written informed consent from all individuals or their legal guardians. Consent for publication: All patients or their legal guardians provided written informed consent for the publication of the research results of this study.
